claims.text: A silicide coating induces controlled silicon diffusion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Silicon diffusion promotes formation of a dual-layer, self-healing scale.
The outer layer is a high-silicon MSi2 layer.
The inner layer is an MSi layer.
Oxidation of the inner layer incorporates (Zr,Hf)O2 particles into the scale.
The dual-layer, self-healing scale governs oxidation resistance and overall material integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The initial material is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy produced by additive manufacturing without a protective surface modification.
Pack cementation can apply a silicide coating to the HfNbTaTiZr alloy and introduce silicon at its surface.
The proposed exposure is approximately 1000°C in flowing air for 20 hours.
Silicon diffusing from the coating reacts with oxygen to form a silicon-rich oxide that protects the substrate.
(Zr,Hf)O2 particles precipitate in cracks formed during thermal cycling and self-seal those cracks.
Silicide-coated samples will have significantly lower mass gain and lower parabolic oxidation-rate constants than uncoated samples.
Silicide-coated samples will exhibit less oxide spallation than uncoated samples.
Silicide-coated samples will form a more continuous and adherent oxide scale containing embedded (Zr,Hf)O2 particles.
The proposed mechanism applies to refractory high-entropy alloys containing sufficient Zr and Hf to form protective oxides when paired with silicon.
The mechanism is expected to hold from approximately 900°C to 1100°C.
The mechanism may differ in alloys lacking the specified compositional features.
Existing studies support enhanced oxidation resistance through silicon diffusion and self-healing oxide formation.
The kinetics of silicon migration and (Zr,Hf)O2 precipitation under varied thermal cycling and environmental conditions remain incompletely quantified.
A controlled comparison uses identically manufactured coated and uncoated HfNbTaTiZr samples exposed at 1000°C in flowing air for 20 hours, with mass gain and scale structure measured.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the MSi2/MSi structure a dual-layer oxide scale, although MSi2 and MSi are silicides; the structural-mediator field separately states that the silicide layers transform into an oxide upon oxidation.
The mechanism invokes cracks formed during thermal cycling, but the stated conditions and falsification experiment specify a static 20-hour oxidation exposure with no thermal-cycling protocol.
